US AQI
info_outline
0-50
Air is clean
It's worth taking a walk or airing out the room.
51-100
Air is moderately clean
Unusually sensitive individuals should consider limiting prolonged exertion especially near busy roads.
101-150
Air is unhealthy for sensitive groups
People with asthma, children and older adults should limit prolonged exertion especially near busy roads.
151-200
Air is unhealthy
People with asthma, children and older adults should avoid prolonged exertion near roadways; everyone else should reduce outdoor exertion.
201-300
Air is very unhealthy
People with asthma, children and older adults should avoid all outdoor exertion; everyone else should avoid prolonged exertion especially near busy roads.
>301
Air is hazardous
Everyone should avoid all outdoor exertion.

What is US AQI?
The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has developed theAir Quality Index. It is based on the measurement of five major pollutants:
  • ground-level ozone (O₃)
  • particle pollution (PM 2.5, PM 10)
  • carbon monoxide (CO)
  • sulfur dioxide (SO₂)
  • nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)
Each pollutant has its own AQI. The highest value is indicated as the overall AQI for the area. The gauge shows a NowCast-style value: PM2.5 is a weighted average of the last 12 hours and CO the mean of the last 8 hours, so one noisy reading does not swing it. The charts show each reading. The higher the AQI value, the higher the level of air pollution and impact on health.
AQI quality levels

thermostat

Temperature

Environmental telemetry • DHT22 sensor (°C)
Description and significance

Measures ambient thermal conditions surrounding the station. In tropical urban environments, ambient temperature directly dictates human thermal comfort, work endurance, and heat stress.

Impact on wireless transmission
Ambient heat changes RF propagation characteristics and causes crystal oscillator drift in the LoRa transceiver. Higher temperatures also accelerate chemical self-discharge in lithium cells and elevate thermal noise in receiver circuits.

Combined with relative humidity, ambient temperature produces the perceived heat index, indicating the body's actual rate of evaporative cooling.

Data quality note: Readings are collected from low-cost sensors uncalibrated against reference standards. Displayed values are indicative for trend awareness and should not be used for regulatory compliance or official health exposure assessment.
Reference thresholds
swap_horiz Swipe table left / right
Range Classification Human sensation
< 20 °C Cool Refreshing, below tropical comfort range
20 to < 30 °C Comfort Tropical outdoor comfort zone (Cameroon field surveys)
30 to < 35 °C Warm Warm discomfort, elevated perspiration
≥ 35 °C Hot Heat exhaustion risk during outdoor exertion (NOAA onset)
Card colour: the card dynamically reflects these sensation bands (cool blue, optimal green, warm amber, hot red).

opacity

Humidity

Relative moisture saturation • DHT22 sensor (%)
Description and particulate relationship

Measures the percentage of water vapor present in the air relative to the saturation limit at the current temperature.

Why humidity matters for PM2.5 readings
The dust sensor measures airborne particles by how much infrared light they scatter. When relative humidity exceeds 70%, microscopic hygroscopic particles absorb moisture and swell. This water swelling causes optical sensors to register larger cross-sections, resulting in elevated raw PM mass estimates during morning mist or rain.

Reviewing humidity alongside PM2.5 confirms whether high particulate readings represent dry combustion smoke or hygroscopically grown aerosol particles.

Data quality note: Readings are collected from low-cost sensors uncalibrated against reference standards. Displayed values are indicative for trend awareness and should not be used for regulatory compliance or official health exposure assessment.

blur_on

Particulate Matter 2.5

Fine inhalable particles • Optical dust sensor (µg/m³)
What is PM2.5?

PM2.5 consists of airborne solid particles and liquid droplets 2.5 micrometers or smaller in diameter (less than 3% the thickness of human hair). Because of their microscopic scale, these particles penetrate deep into lung alveoli and cross into the bloodstream.

Primary emission sources
  • 🚗
    Road transport: Diesel soot, unburned fuel from congested traffic, and brake pad erosion.
  • 🔥
    Open burning: Backyard rubbish fires, agricultural clearing, and dry bush burns.
  • 🪵
    Domestic fuels: Charcoal stoves and wood fires used for roadside kitchens.
  • 💨
    Road dust: Resuspended mineral soil from unpaved roads and construction sites.
WHO guideline: the 2021 WHO guideline is an annual mean below 5 µg/m³ and a 24-hour mean below 15 µg/m³. The 24-hour value falls inside the EPA Moderate band, so a reading can be EPA Moderate and still exceed the WHO guideline.
Data quality note: Readings are collected from low-cost optical sensors (GP2Y1010AU0F) uncalibrated against reference standards. Displayed values are indicative for trend awareness and should not be used for regulatory compliance. EPA breakpoints are defined for 24-hour averages and applied here to a 12-hour NowCast.
Health impact bands (US EPA table, May 2024)

cloud

Carbon Monoxide

Toxic combustion gas • Gas sensor (ppm)
What is carbon monoxide?

Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas produced by incomplete combustion of carbon-based fuels. When inhaled, it binds to blood hemoglobin with 200 times the affinity of oxygen, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of arterial blood.

Primary emission sources
  • 🚙
    Idling vehicles: Old carbureted engines, heavy lorries, and motorcycle taxis in slow traffic.
  • ⚡
    Generators: Small gasoline and diesel generators operated during local power cuts.
  • 🍳
    Charcoal cooking: Enclosed or poorly ventilated charcoal braziers and wood hearths.
Data quality note: Readings are collected from low-cost sensors uncalibrated against reference standards. Displayed values are indicative for trend awareness and should not be used for regulatory compliance or official health exposure assessment. The card shows the mean of the last 8 hours, the EPA averaging time for CO, and needs data in at least 6 of those 8 hours.

done_all

Packet Delivery Rate

Network telemetry • Uplink reliability (%)
Everyday analogy
Postal delivery success rate
Think of a postman delivering letters. If a sensor mails 100 letters and the gateway receives 97 in its mailbox, the delivery ratio is 97%. Missing letters were lost to collisions, weak signal, or interference.
How is it calculated?

Every LoRaWAN packet carries an incrementing frame counter (f_cnt). The rule chain looks at the last 20 frames, taken from the previous 180 minutes of history, and divides the frames that arrived by the number the counter says were sent.

A high value means the recent frames all arrived.

Reading a low value: PDR is inferred from counter gaps, so it can drop without packet loss. For example, if a node's transmit interval changes, a counter resets, or a device rejoins, the calculation registers a transient drop even when no radio frames were lost.
Operational evaluation
swap_horiz Swipe table left / right
Ratio Health status Operational interpretation
≥ 80% Good Most expected frames arrived
60 to < 80% Degraded Frequent gaps; compare with RSSI and SNR
< 60% Poor Many frames missing; check RSSI, SNR and the uplink history before moving anything
Card colour: green at 80% or more, amber at 60% or more, red below.

battery_std

Battery

Power telemetry • Voltage & State of Charge
Everyday analogy
Fuel level and pump pressure
Voltage represents electrical pressure; State of Charge (SoC %) represents how much usable energy is left in the tank. When electrical pressure drops too low, the node can no longer run its sensors or transmit reliably.
How is it measured?

The microcontroller reads the battery voltage through a resistor divider on an ADC pin. The rule chain converts the reading to volts, then maps 3.3 V to 0% and 4.2 V to 100% in a straight line. A real Li-ion cell does not discharge linearly, so the percentage is an estimate, useful mainly for spotting a low battery.

Firmware guard: the node has its own low-battery guard, set in raw ADC counts rather than volts and adjustable by downlink. In low-battery mode it powers off the dust and gas sensors. The dashboard percentage and this table are display thresholds, separate from that guard.

signal_cellular_alt

Received Signal Strength Indicator

Radio physical layer • Power at gateway (dBm)
Everyday analogy
Shouting vs whispering
RSSI is how loud the sensor sounds at the gateway antenna. A sensor next door speaks at a loud volume (-70 dBm). A station several kilometers away through concrete buildings arrives as a faint whisper (-118 dBm).
Measurement principle

Measured in negative decibel-milliwatts (dBm) by the gateway transceiver chipset upon packet reception. Closer to 0 represents a stronger radio signal.

Because decibels are logarithmic, every 3 dB drop represents a 50% decrease in received radio power.

Receiver limit: for a 125 kHz LoRa channel, receiver sensitivity runs from about -123 dBm at SF7 to about -137 dBm at SF12. A weak reading at a high spreading factor can still be decoded.
Signal strength bands
swap_horiz Swipe table left / right
Power Category Radio link margin
≥ -90 dBm Strong High signal margin; direct line of sight
-110 to < -90 dBm Normal Typical urban propagation range
< -110 dBm Weak Building penetration loss; marginal link
Card colour: green at -90 dBm or above, amber at -110 or above, red below.

graphic_eq

Signal-to-Noise Ratio

Demodulation clarity • Signal vs noise (dB)
Everyday analogy
Talking in a busy market
RSSI is how loud someone speaks; SNR is how clearly you hear them over the marketplace noise. A positive SNR means their voice is louder than the crowd. A negative SNR means the background noise is louder than their voice.
The LoRa chirp spread spectrum advantage

Conventional radio protocols fail when noise exceeds signal (negative SNR). LoRa uses Chirp Spread Spectrum modulation, so the receiver can decode signals below the noise floor. How far below depends on the spreading factor: about -7.5 dB at SF7, down to -20 dB at SF12.

Demodulation limit by spreading factor (125 kHz): SF7 -7.5 dB, SF8 -10 dB, SF9 -12.5 dB, SF10 -15 dB, SF11 -17.5 dB, SF12 -20 dB.
Clarity evaluation bands
swap_horiz Swipe table left / right
SNR (dB) Condition Demodulation margin
≥ +5 dB Clean Signal well above the noise
-10 to < +5 dB Marginal Signal near or below the noise; LoRa still decodes, depending on spreading factor
< -10 dB Poor Beyond the limit of SF7 and SF8; only SF9 to SF12 can still decode
Card colour: green at +5 dB or above, amber at -10 dB or above, red below.
